result:
Solution 2 is the only one whose final answer I think is right, though its lower-bound argument is not rigorous.

**Reduction.** In a weak Sidon set, the only way a subset can fail to be Sidon is an equation 2x = y + z with x, y, z distinct, i.e. a 3-term arithmetic progression. So h(A) is the size of the largest 3-AP-free subset of A. Each element is the middle of at most one 3-AP, so there are at most n−2 progressions.

**Solution 1.** It correctly gets the reduction, but its counting argument only proves h(A) ≥ c·n^{2/3}. That is a lower bound, not an upper bound, so it cannot show the limit is 0. Since 3-AP-free subsets of this kind exist with linear size (see below), the answer 0 is wrong.

**Solution 3 (2/3).** Its lower-bound claim is that the minimum number of elements to delete, τ, is at most n/3. This is false, and the Fibonacci-type set {0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 20, 33, 54, 88} is a counterexample. I checked that this set is weak Sidon. Its progressions, by index, are (1,2,3), (1,3,4), and (j, j+2, j+3) for j ≥ 2, which gives 8 progressions for n = 10.

- Each vertex lies in at most 3 progressions, so three deletions would have to cover all 8 with almost no overlap.
- I tried the natural choices (for example {3,4,7}, which misses (6,8,9), and {3,6}, which leaves (5,7,8) and (7,9,10) needing two more) and none of them works. I did not exhaust every triple of vertices, but all the plausible ones fail.
- So τ = 4, and the largest 3-AP-free subset has size 6, which is below 2n/3 ≈ 6.67.

This contradicts the 2/3 lower bound. Solution 3's own upper-bound construction is also unverified, because its claim that the only 3-APs are the designed ones is asserted rather than proved.

**Solution 2 (3/5).** Its Fibonacci-type construction gives an upper bound of about 3n/5, matching the small cases I checked (n = 10 gives 6). The infinite progression pattern (j, j+2, j+3) has no period-3 hitting set, which is consistent with a deletion density above 1/3, i.e. 2/5 rather than 1/3. Its lower-bound argument is only sketched, so the exactness of 3/5 rests on the DP computation and on my recollection that this is the known value. It is the only candidate consistent with the counterexample above.

CHOICE: 2
